Abstract algebra studies structures: a set together with one or more operations that obey a short list of rules. Instead of asking "what is 7⋅13?", it asks "which facts about multiplication follow from the rules alone, so that they hold for integers, for clock arithmetic, for matrices, for symmetries of a molecule, all at once?". That shift pays off in many places: symmetry (crystallography, chemistry, physics), cryptography (RSA and elliptic-curve systems are group theory in disguise), coding theory (error-correcting codes on every phone and disk are built over finite fields), and the classical question of solving polynomial equations, which Galois settled with groups. This series follows the standard senior undergraduate path of Dummit & Foote, Gallian, Artin and Fraleigh: groups, then rings and fields, then Galois theory. Post 00 lays the ground: the proof methods used throughout, sets and functions, equivalence relations, and the arithmetic of the integers up to modular arithmetic, the Chinese remainder theorem and a small but complete RSA example. Every later post uses Z and Z/nZ as its first examples.
Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic (this post) → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory.

Read and write the four basic proof patterns: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction.
Decide whether a function is injective, surjective or bijective, and use the fact that bijections are exactly the invertible functions.
Prove that an equivalence relation on a set is the same thing as a partition of that set.
State and prove the division algorithm from the well-ordering principle.
Run the Euclidean algorithm and the extended Euclidean algorithm by hand, and prove Bézout's identity and Euclid's lemma.
Prove the fundamental theorem of arithmetic (existence and uniqueness).
Compute in Z/nZ, find inverses, and decide which classes are units.
Use Euler's φ function, Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem to reduce huge powers.
Solve simultaneous congruences with the Chinese remainder theorem.
Carry out a toy RSA key generation, encryption and decryption, and explain why decryption works.
Abstract algebra is a proof-based subject. Almost every statement is an implication "if P then Q", and there are four standard ways to prove one.

Proposition / theorem / lemma / corollary — a proved statement; a lemma is a helper, a corollary follows quickly from a theorem.
Definition — fixes the meaning of a word. Definitions are "if and only if" even when written with "if".
Contrapositive of "P⇒Q" is "not Q⇒ not P". It is logically equivalent to the original.
Converse of "P⇒Q" is "Q⇒P". It is a different statement and may be false.
Counterexample — one concrete case that shows a universal statement is false.

Assume P, reason forward, reach Q.
Claim. The sum of two odd integers is even.
Proof. Odd integers can be written 2a+1 and 2b+1 with a,b∈Z. Their sum is 2a+2b+2=2(a+b+1), which is even. ■

Prove "not Q⇒ not P" instead.
Claim. If n2 is even, then n is even.
Proof. Contrapositive: if n is odd then n2 is odd. Write n=2k+1; then n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1, which is odd. ■

Assume the statement is false and derive something impossible.
Claim. 2 is irrational.
Proof. Suppose 2=p/q with integers p,q, q≠0, and the fraction in lowest terms. Then p2=2q2, so p2 is even, so p is even by the previous claim. Write p=2m: then 4m2=2q2, so q2=2m2 is even and q is even. Both p and q are even, contradicting lowest terms. ■

To prove a statement S(n) for all integers n≥n0: prove S(n0) (the base case), then prove S(k)⇒S(k+1) for every k≥n0 (the inductive step). In strong induction the inductive step may assume S(n0),…,S(k) all at once.
Claim. For every n≥1, 1+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n2.
Proof. Base case n=1: 1=12. Inductive step: if the sum of the first k odd numbers is k2, adding the next one gives k2+(2k+1)=(k+1)2. ■
Watch out: proving the converse is not proving the statement. "If n is even then n2 is even" is true, but it does not prove "if n2 is even then n is even"; that needed its own proof above.

N={0,1,2,… } (some books start at 1; this series includes 0), Z the integers, Q the rationals, R the reals, C the complex numbers.
A×B={(a,b):a∈A,b∈B} is the Cartesian product.
A function f:A→B assigns to each a∈A exactly one f(a)∈B. A is the domain, B the codomain, f(A) the image.
f is injective (one-to-one) if f(a1)=f(a2) implies a1=a2.
f is surjective (onto) if every b∈B equals f(a) for some a.
f is bijective if it is both. A bijection from a set to itself is a permutation of the set.
A relation on A is a subset R⊆A×A; write a∼b when (a,b)∈R.

Examples on Z: f(x)=2x is injective but not surjective (odd numbers are missed). g(x)=⌊x/2⌋ is surjective but not injective (g(0)=g(1)=0). h(x)=x+5 is bijective with inverse x↦x−5.
Proposition 2.1. A function f:A→B has an inverse function g:B→A (with g∘f=idA and f∘g=idB) if and only if f is bijective.
Proof. If g exists: f(a1)=f(a2) gives a1=g(f(a1))=g(f(a2))=a2, so f is injective; and any b equals f(g(b)), so f is surjective. Conversely, if f is bijective, each b has exactly one preimage; define g(b) to be it. Then both compositions are identities. ■
Proposition 2.2 (pigeonhole). If A is a finite set and f:A→A is injective, then f is bijective.
Proof. An injective f sends the ∣A∣ elements of A to ∣A∣ distinct elements of A, so the image is all of A. ■
This small fact drives the proofs of Fermat's little theorem below and of Cayley's theorem later in the series. It is false for infinite sets: x↦2x on Z is injective but not surjective.

A relation ∼ on A is an equivalence relation if it is
reflexive: a∼a for all a;
symmetric: a∼b implies b∼a;
transitive: a∼b and b∼c imply a∼c.
The equivalence class of a is [a]={x∈A:x∼a}.
Examples: equality on any set; "same birthday" on people; "a−b is divisible by n" on Z (Chapter 5); "same determinant" on 2×2 matrices. Non-examples: ≤ on R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; "∣a−b∣≤1" on R is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive (0∼1, 1∼2, but 0≁2).
A partition of A is a collection of non-empty subsets of A such that every element of A lies in exactly one of them.
Theorem 2.3 (equivalence relations = partitions). If ∼ is an equivalence relation on A, its equivalence classes form a partition of A. Conversely, every partition P of A comes from exactly one equivalence relation: a∼b if and only if a and b lie in the same block of P.
Proof. Each class is non-empty and every a lies in a class, because a∈[a] by reflexivity. It remains to show that two classes are either equal or disjoint. Suppose c∈[a]∩[b], so c∼a and c∼b. Take any x∈[a]: then x∼a, a∼c (symmetry), c∼b, so x∼b by transitivity twice, and x∈[b]. Hence [a]⊆[b], and by the same argument [b]⊆[a]. So overlapping classes are equal.
Conversely, given a partition, "same block" is reflexive (every element is in a block), symmetric (obvious), and transitive (if a,b share block P and b,c share block Q, then b∈P∩Q, so P=Q because blocks are disjoint). Its classes are exactly the blocks. ■
Trick: to show two classes are equal it is enough to find one common element. This "one overlap means equal" step is used again for cosets in post 02, where it gives Lagrange's theorem almost for free.

a divides b, written a∣b, if b=ak for some integer k. Every integer divides 0; 0 divides only 0.
A prime is an integer p≥2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p. An integer n≥2 that is not prime is composite.
The greatest common divisor gcd⁡(a,b) of integers not both zero is the largest integer dividing both. Set gcd⁡(0,0)=0.
a and b are coprime (relatively prime) if gcd⁡(a,b)=1.
Well-ordering principle: every non-empty set of non-negative integers has a least element. It is equivalent to induction and is taken as an axiom about N.

Theorem 3.1 (division algorithm). For integers a and b with b>0 there are unique integers q,r with
a=qb+r,0≤r<b.
Proof. Existence: let S={a−kb:k∈Z, a−kb≥0}. S is non-empty (take k=−∣a∣; then a−kb=a+∣a∣b≥a+∣a∣≥0). By well-ordering S has a least element r=a−qb≥0. If r≥b, then r−b=a−(q+1)b is a smaller element of S, a contradiction. So 0≤r<b.
Uniqueness: if qb+r=q′b+r′ with both remainders in [0,b), then b(q−q′)=r′−r and ∣r′−r∣<b. The only multiple of b strictly between −b and b is 0, so r=r′ and q=q′. ■
For negative a the remainder is still non-negative: −17=(−4)⋅5+3, not (−3)⋅5−2.
Common pitfall: in many programming languages -17 % 5 returns -2 (C, Java, JavaScript) while Python returns 3. Mathematics always uses 0≤r<b.

Lemma 3.2. If a=qb+r, then gcd⁡(a,b)=gcd⁡(b,r).
Proof. Any common divisor of a and b divides r=a−qb; any common divisor of b and r divides a=qb+r. The two pairs have the same common divisors, so the same greatest one. ■
Repeating the division algorithm, the remainders strictly decrease and so reach 0; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd. For gcd⁡(240,46):
240=5⋅46+1046=4⋅10+610=1⋅6+46=1⋅4+24=2⋅2+0
So gcd⁡(240,46)=2. The number of steps is small: it grows like the number of digits (Lamé's theorem bounds it by five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number).

Theorem 3.3 (Bézout). For integers a,b not both zero, there are integers x,y with ax+by=gcd⁡(a,b). Moreover gcd⁡(a,b) is the smallest positive integer of the form ax+by.
Proof. Let S={ax+by:x,y∈Z}∩{1,2,3,… }. It is non-empty (it contains a2+b2>0), so it has a least element d=ax0+by0. Divide: a=qd+r with 0≤r<d. Then r=a−q(ax0+by0)=a(1−qx0)+b(−qy0) has the same form, so by minimality r=0 and d∣a. Likewise d∣b. Any common divisor c of a,b divides ax0+by0=d, so c≤d. Hence d=gcd⁡(a,b). ■
The proof shows x,y exist but does not find them. The extended Euclidean algorithm does: keep, next to every remainder ri, integers si,ti with ri=240si+46ti. Start with r0=240=240⋅1+46⋅0 and r1=46=240⋅0+46⋅1; each new row is "row two above minus q times row above".
i · ri · qi · si · ti · check 240si+46ti
0 · 240 · — · 1 · 0 · 240
1 · 46 · — · 0 · 1 · 46
2 · 10 · 5 · 1 · −5 · 240 − 230 = 10
3 · 6 · 4 · −4 · 21 · −960 + 966 = 6
4 · 4 · 1 · 5 · −26 · 1200 − 1196 = 4
5 · 2 · 1 · −9 · 47 · −2160 + 2162 = 2
6 · 0 · 2 · — · — · stop
So 2=240⋅(−9)+46⋅47. The same answer comes from back-substitution, reading the divisions from the bottom up: 2=6−4=6−(10−6)=2⋅6−10=2(46−4⋅10)−10=2⋅46−9⋅10=2⋅46−9(240−5⋅46)=47⋅46−9⋅240.
Trick: the x,y are not unique: (x+23k, y−120k) works for every integer k, because 240⋅23=46⋅120. Add a check column like the one above; one wrong sign early ruins every later row.

Theorem 3.4 (Euclid's lemma). If a∣bc and gcd⁡(a,b)=1, then a∣c. In particular, if a prime p divides bc, then p∣b or p∣c.
Proof. By Bézout, ax+by=1 for some x,y. Multiply by c: c=acx+bcy. The number a divides acx and divides bcy (because a∣bc), so a∣c. For the prime case: if p∤b then gcd⁡(p,b)=1 (the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p), so p∣c. ■
Watch out: the prime hypothesis matters. 6∣4⋅9=36 but 6∤4 and 6∤9.

Theorem 4.1 (fundamental theorem of arithmetic). Every integer n≥2 can be written as a product of primes n=p1p2⋯pk, and this factorisation is unique up to the order of the factors.
Proof. Existence, by strong induction on n. If n is prime, it is its own factorisation. Otherwise n=ab with 2≤a,b<n; by the induction hypothesis both a and b are products of primes, so n is too.
Uniqueness, by induction on n. Suppose n=p1⋯pk=q1⋯ql with all pi,qj prime. Then p1 divides q1⋯ql, so by Euclid's lemma (applied repeatedly) p1∣qj for some j. Since qj is prime and p1≥2, p1=qj. Reorder so that j=1 and cancel: p2⋯pk=q2⋯ql is a smaller number (or both sides are empty products equal to 1), and by induction the remaining primes agree up to order. ■
Grouping equal primes gives the canonical form n=p1e1⋯prer with p1<⋯<pr. Examples: 360=23⋅32⋅5, 1001=7⋅11⋅13, 2026=2⋅1013.
Corollary 4.2 (Euclid). There are infinitely many primes.
Proof. Given primes p1,…,pk, the number N=p1⋯pk+1 has a prime factor p by Theorem 4.1. If p were some pi, then p would divide N−p1⋯pk=1, which is impossible. So no finite list contains every prime. ■
Uniqueness is not automatic. In the set {a+b−5:a,b∈Z}, 6=2⋅3=(1+−5)(1−−5) gives two genuinely different factorisations into elements that cannot be split further. Explaining when unique factorisation holds is one of the main themes of ring theory (post 04).

Fix an integer n≥1, the modulus. a is congruent to b modulo n, written a≡b(modn), if n∣a−b.
The class of a is [a]n={a+kn:k∈Z}, also written aˉ or just a when the modulus is clear.
Z/nZ (also written Zn) is the set of the n classes [0],[1],…,[n−1].
A class [a] is a unit if there is [b] with [a][b]=[1]. The units form (Z/nZ)×, also written U(n).
A non-zero class [a] is a zero divisor if [a][b]=[0] for some non-zero [b].
Congruence mod n is an equivalence relation: n∣0 (reflexive); n∣a−b implies n∣b−a (symmetric); n∣a−b and n∣b−c imply n∣a−c (transitive). By Theorem 2.3 its classes partition Z, and by the division algorithm each class contains exactly one of 0,1,…,n−1, so there are exactly n classes.

Define [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a]⋅[b]=[ab].
Proposition 5.1. These operations are well defined: the result does not depend on which representatives are chosen.
Proof. Suppose a≡a′ and b≡b′, say a′=a+kn and b′=b+ln. Then a′+b′=a+b+(k+l)n≡a+b and a′b′=ab+(al+bk+kln)n≡ab. ■
"Well defined" is the central worry whenever an operation is defined on classes through representatives. The same check, done for cosets, is what forces the definition of a normal subgroup in post 02.
In practice: reduce early and often. For example 3100 mod 7: 36≡1(mod7) (checked below), and 100=6⋅16+4, so 3100=(36)16⋅34≡34=81≡4(mod7).

In Z/12Z: [3][4]=[12]=[0], so [3] and [4] are zero divisors. On the other hand [5][5]=[25]=[1], [7][7]=[49]=[1] and [11][11]=[121]=[1]. The units are exactly [1],[5],[7],[11], the classes coprime to 12, and each of them is its own inverse.
Theorem 5.2. [a] is a unit in Z/nZ if and only if gcd⁡(a,n)=1. If gcd⁡(a,n)=d>1 and n∤a, then [a] is a zero divisor.
Proof. If gcd⁡(a,n)=1, Bézout gives ax+ny=1, so ax≡1 and [x] is the inverse. Conversely if ab≡1, then ab−1=kn, so ab−kn=1 and every common divisor of a and n divides 1. For the last claim: a⋅(n/d)=(a/d)⋅n≡0, and [n/d]≠[0] because 0<n/d<n. ■
Corollary 5.3. Z/nZ has every non-zero class invertible if and only if n is prime.
Theorem 5.2 is also an algorithm: the inverse is the Bézout coefficient. To invert 17 modulo 43: 43=2⋅17+9, 17=1⋅9+8, 9=1⋅8+1. Back-substitute: 1=9−8=9−(17−9)=2⋅9−17=2(43−2⋅17)−17=2⋅43−5⋅17. So 17−1≡−5≡38(mod43). Check: 17⋅38=646=15⋅43+1.

Theorem 5.4. The congruence ax≡b(modn) has a solution if and only if d=gcd⁡(a,n) divides b. In that case it has exactly d solutions modulo n.
Proof sketch. A solution means ax−ny=b for some y, and by Bézout the values of ax−ny are exactly the multiples of d. If d∣b, divide through: (a/d)x≡b/d(modn/d), and a/d is a unit mod n/d, so x is unique mod n/d. That single class mod n/d splits into d classes mod n. ■
Example: 14x≡6(mod20). Here gcd⁡(14,20)=2 divides 6. Divide by 2: 7x≡3(mod10). Since 7⋅3=21≡1, 7−1≡3(mod10), so x≡9(mod10), giving x≡9 or 19(mod20). Check: 14⋅9=126=6⋅20+6 and 14⋅19=266=13⋅20+6.
Common pitfall: you may not "divide both sides" of a congruence by a number that is not a unit. 2⋅3≡2⋅9(mod12), but 3≢9(mod12). Division by a modulo n is multiplication by a−1, which exists only when gcd⁡(a,n)=1; otherwise the modulus must be divided too, as above.

φ(n) is the number of integers in {1,…,n} coprime to n; by Theorem 5.2 it is the number of units, φ(n)=∣(Z/nZ)×∣.
For a prime p: φ(p)=p−1.
For a prime power: φ(pk)=pk−pk−1, because the numbers in {1,…,pk} not coprime to pk are exactly the pk−1 multiples of p.
Multiplicative: if gcd⁡(m,n)=1 then φ(mn)=φ(m)φ(n). This follows from the Chinese remainder theorem (Chapter 7): a is coprime to mn exactly when it is coprime to both m and n, and the CRT bijection matches such a with pairs of units.
Together these give, for n=p1e1⋯prer,
φ(n)=n∏p∣n(1−1p).
Examples: φ(12)=12⋅12⋅23=4 (the units 1,5,7,11); φ(36)=36⋅12⋅23=12; φ(100)=100⋅12⋅45=40; φ(35)=φ(5)φ(7)=4⋅6=24.

Theorem 6.1 (Fermat's little theorem). If p is prime and p∤a, then ap−1≡1(modp). Consequently ap≡a(modp) for every integer a.
Proof. Consider the map x↦ax on the set R={[1],[2],…,[p−1]} of non-zero classes mod p. It lands in R (a product of two units is a unit, so never [0]) and is injective, because ax≡ay implies x≡y after multiplying by a−1. By the pigeonhole Proposition 2.2 it is a bijection, so it just reorders R. Multiply all elements of R both ways:
(a⋅1)(a⋅2)⋯(a⋅(p−1))≡1⋅2⋯(p−1)(modp),
that is ap−1(p−1)!≡(p−1)!(modp). Every factor of (p−1)! is a unit, so (p−1)! is a unit and can be cancelled: ap−1≡1. For the second statement multiply by a; if p∣a both sides are 0. ■
Check with p=7, a=3: multiplying 1,2,3,4,5,6 by 3 gives 3,6,2,5,1,4 modulo 7, the same six classes in a new order, and 36=729=104⋅7+1.

Theorem 6.2 (Euler). If gcd⁡(a,n)=1, then aφ(n)≡1(modn).
Proof. Repeat the proof above with the set U of the φ(n) units mod n instead of R: x↦ax permutes U, so aφ(n)∏u∈Uu≡∏u∈Uu, and the product of units is a unit, so it cancels. ■
Fermat is the case n=p. Post 02 re-proves both in one line from Lagrange's theorem, because (Z/nZ)× is a group of order φ(n) and the order of an element divides the order of the group.
Example: the last digit of 7222. φ(10)=4 and gcd⁡(7,10)=1, so 74≡1(mod10). Since 222=4⋅55+2, 7222≡72=49≡9. The last digit is 9.
Watch out: Euler's theorem needs gcd⁡(a,n)=1. 2φ(4)=22=4≡0(mod4), not 1. Also, φ(n) is an exponent that always works, not always the smallest one: modulo 12, every unit already satisfies u2≡1 although φ(12)=4.

Theorem 7.1 (Chinese remainder theorem). Let n1,…,nk be pairwise coprime positive integers and N=n1⋯nk. For any integers a1,…,ak the system
x≡a1(modn1),…,x≡ak(modnk)
has a solution, and any two solutions are congruent modulo N.
Proof. Existence: put Ni=N/ni. Since ni is coprime to every other nj, it is coprime to Ni, so there is Mi with NiMi≡1(modni). Let x=∑iaiNiMi. Modulo nj, every term with i≠j vanishes (because nj∣Ni), and the j-th term is aj⋅1. Uniqueness: if x,x′ both work, each ni divides x−x′; the ni are pairwise coprime, so (by Euclid's lemma, repeatedly) their product N divides x−x′. ■
Worked example (Sunzi's classic puzzle). Find x with x≡2(mod3), x≡3(mod5), x≡2(mod7). Here N=105.
i · ni · ai · Ni=N/ni · Ni mod ni · Mi · aiNiMi
1 · 3 · 2 · 35 · 2 · 2 · 140
2 · 5 · 3 · 21 · 1 · 1 · 63
3 · 7 · 2 · 15 · 1 · 1 · 30
Sum: 140+63+30=233≡23(mod105). Check: 23=7⋅3+2, 23=4⋅5+3, 23=3⋅7+2.
In structural language, the theorem says that the map Z/NZ→Z/n1Z×⋯×Z/nkZ, [x]↦([x]n1,…,[x]nk), is a bijection that respects addition and multiplication. Both sides have N elements, so it is enough to know the map is injective, which is the uniqueness part. Post 01 meets the additive version as "Z/6Z is the same group as Z/2Z×Z/3Z", and post 04 the ring version.
Common pitfall: the moduli must be pairwise coprime. The system x≡0(mod4), x≡1(mod6) has no solution: the first says x is even, the second says x is odd.

RSA (Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 1978) is Euler's theorem put to work. The numbers below are tiny so that every step can be checked by hand; real keys use primes of about 1024 bits or more and a padding scheme, and textbook RSA as shown here is not secure.
Key generation.
Pick primes p=11, q=17. The modulus is n=pq=187.
φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1)=10⋅16=160.
Pick a public exponent e coprime to 160: e=7.
The private exponent is d=e−1 mod φ(n): since 7⋅23=161=160+1, d=23.
Public key (n,e)=(187,7); private key d=23.
Encryption of the message m=88 (any integer with 0≤m<n): c=me mod n, computed by repeated squaring so that no number exceeds 1862:
882=7744≡77(mod187)884≡772=5929≡132887=884⋅882⋅88≡132⋅77⋅88≡66⋅88=5808≡11
So the ciphertext is c=11.
Decryption: cd=1123 mod 187. Write 23=16+4+2+1 and square repeatedly: 112=121, 114≡1212=14641≡55, 118≡552=3025≡33, 1116≡332=1089≡154. Then
1123≡154⋅55⋅121⋅11≡55⋅121⋅11≡110⋅11=1210≡88(mod187).
The original message comes back.
Why it works. ed=1+kφ(n) for some k≥0. If gcd⁡(m,n)=1, Euler gives med=m⋅(mφ(n))k≡m(modn). (If m shares a factor with n, the result still holds: check it modulo p and modulo q separately with Fermat, then combine with the CRT.)
Why it is believed hard to break. Anyone who knows φ(n) can compute d with the extended Euclidean algorithm, and φ(n) is easy from p and q. So the security rests on the difficulty of factoring n; no fast classical factoring algorithm is known.

1. Prove by induction that 6∣n3−n for every integer n≥0.
Solution
Base: 03−0=0. Step: (k+1)3−(k+1)=(k3−k)+3k2+3k=(k3−k)+3k(k+1). The first term is divisible by 6 by hypothesis; k(k+1) is a product of consecutive integers, hence even, so 3k(k+1) is divisible by 6. (A direct proof also works: n3−n=(n−1)n(n+1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 2 and by 3.)
2. On R2 define (x1,y1)∼(x2,y2) if x12+y12=x22+y22. Show this is an equivalence relation and describe the partition.
Solution
It is "f(p1)=f(p2)" for the function f(x,y)=x2+y2, and any relation of that form inherits reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity from equality. The classes are the circles centred at the origin, plus the single point (0,0).
3. Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to find gcd⁡(252,198) and integers x,y with 252x+198y=gcd⁡(252,198).
Solution
252=1⋅198+54, 198=3⋅54+36, 54=1⋅36+18, 36=2⋅18. So the gcd is 18. Back-substitute: 18=54−36=54−(198−3⋅54)=4⋅54−198=4(252−198)−198=4⋅252−5⋅198. Check: 1008−990=18.
4. Find all solutions of 14x≡6(mod20) by the method of Theorem 5.4, and explain why 14x≡5(mod20) has none.
Solution
As in Chapter 5: x≡9 or 19(mod20). For the second congruence, gcd⁡(14,20)=2 does not divide 5: the left side 14x−20y is always even, the right side is odd.
5. Compute 21000 mod 13 and the last two digits of 32026.
Solution
By Fermat 212≡1(mod13); 1000=12⋅83+4, so

5: x≡9 or 19(mod20). For the second congruence, gcd⁡(14,20)=2 does not divide 5: the left side 14x−20y is always even, the right side is odd.
5. Compute 21000 mod 13 and the last two digits of 32026.
Solution
By Fermat 212≡1(mod13); 1000=12⋅83+4, so 21000≡24=16≡3. For the last two digits work mod 100: φ(100)=40 and gcd⁡(3,100)=1, so 340≡1; 2026=40⋅50+26, so 32026≡326. Now 35=243≡43, 310≡432=1849≡49, 320≡492=2401≡1. (The order of 3 mod 100 is actually 20, a divisor of 40.) So 326≡36=729≡29. The last two digits are 29.
6. Solve x≡3(mod4), x≡4(mod9).
Solution
N=36. N1=9≡1(mod4), so M1=1; N2=4 and 4⋅7=28≡1(mod9), so M2=7. Then x=3⋅9⋅1+4⋅4⋅7=27+112=139≡31(mod36). Check: 31=7⋅4+3 and 31=3⋅9+4.
7. With p=5, q=11 and e=3, find n, φ(n) and d; encrypt m=7 and decrypt the result.
Solution
n=55, φ(n)=4⋅10=40, d=27 because 3⋅27=81=2⋅40+1. Encrypt: 73=343=6⋅55+13, so c=13. Decrypt: 132=169≡4, 134≡16, 138≡256≡36, 1316≡362=1296≡31. With 27=16+8+2+1: 31⋅36=1116≡16, 16⋅4=64≡9, 9⋅13=117≡7. The message 7 comes back.

Post 01 takes the pattern seen here (a set, one operation, an identity, inverses) and turns it into the definition of a group. Z under addition, Z/nZ under addition and (Z/nZ)× under multiplication become the first examples, joined by permutations, symmetries of polygons, invertible matrices and the quaternions. The division algorithm reappears in the proof that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, and gcd⁡ returns in the formula n/gcd⁡(k,n) for the order of k in Z/nZ.
